title: How do you decide whether a private equity fund should invest in a company?
description: "Should the fund invest in this company?" Private equity: a fund buys a company to improve it and sell it in 3 to 7 years.
hook: Decide whether a private equity fund should invest by working back from the return it needs: what must the company be worth when the fund sells, and is that a realistic plan from where the business starts today? Around that calculation sit four checks: an attractive market, a strong company, clear ways to add value, and a credible buyer at exit.
body:
When you will use it

A private equity fund wants to buy a company, improve it and sell it, usually within three to seven years. The prompt is "Should the fund buy X?" or "Can the fund make 3x on this deal?"

It looks like an acquisition case, with one big difference. A company buying a rival plans to own it for ever and can count synergies. A fund plans to sell, so everything comes back to the exit: who buys the business, at what price, and what return that gives. This is a decide question, so end with a clear yes or no. More on the three families of case questions.

Ask this first

What return does the fund need, over how many years, and how much of the price is funded with debt?

Returns are measured two ways. The money multiple (MOIC) is equity received at exit divided by equity invested. The IRR is the annual return that multiple implies. Useful pairs to know: 2x over five years is about 15% a year, 2.5x is about 20%, 3x is about 25%. Tripling your money over six years is also about 20%.

The structure

  • Is the market attractive?
    • Size and growth
    • Margins
    • Barriers to entry
  • Is the company strong?
    • Position against competitors
    • Performance and outlook
    • Management team
  • How can we add value?
    • Grow revenue
    • Raise margins
    • Buy add-on companies
    • Pay down debt from cash flow
  • Can we exit well? (this gives the return)
    • Who would buy it
    • Exit multiple
    • Timing

For a quick read on how industry structure affects the first branch, see Porter's five forces.

A worked example: work back from the return

The illustrative facts: a business earns $8M of EBITDA and can be bought for 10x, an enterprise value of $80M. The fund puts in $40M of equity and borrows $40M. It plans to sell after five years and targets 2.5x its money.

Step 1: equity needed at exit

$40M × 2.5 = $100M of equity proceeds. That is about 20% a year.

Step 2: enterprise value needed at exit

Equity is what is left after repaying debt. If cash flow pays the debt down from $40M to $20M by exit, the business must sell for $100M + $20M = $120M.

Step 3: EBITDA needed at exit

If buyers still pay 10x, the company needs $120M ÷ 10 = $12M of EBITDA, up from $8M. That is 50% growth over five years, about 8.4% a year. The case now has a precise question: can this business realistically grow profit by roughly 8% a year?

Step 4: show where the value comes from

SourceCalculationEquity gain
EBITDA growth($12M − $8M) × 10$40M
Debt paydown$40M − $20M$20M
Change in multipleAssumed none$0M
Total$100M − $40M$60M

This value bridge is what interviewers want to see. A plan that depends on the exit multiple rising is betting on the market, not on the fund's own work.

Step 5: test the downside

Suppose EBITDA reaches only $10M and buyers pay 9x. Enterprise value is $90M; after $20M of debt, equity is $70M. That is 1.75x, about 12% a year, well short of the target. If the fund still wants the deal, it needs a lower entry price or more confidence in the growth plan.

What a strong answer sounds like

"To make 2.5x, the fund needs $100M of equity at exit, so with $20M of debt left the business must sell for $120M. At 10x that means $12M of EBITDA, up from $8M, or about 8% growth a year. Two-thirds of the gain comes from profit growth and a third from paying down debt. If growth stalls at $10M and the multiple slips to 9x, we make only 1.75x, so I'd invest only if we can see a clear path to that growth, or if we can buy for less."

A weak answer spends five minutes on the market, says "it looks like a good company" and never calculates the return.

Common mistakes

  • Never calculating the return. The return is the answer to a PE case. Get to it early.
  • Confusing equity and enterprise value. Exit equity is enterprise value minus remaining debt.
  • Relying on multiple expansion. Assume the exit multiple is the same as, or lower than, the entry multiple unless there is a reason.
  • Forgetting the exit. Name likely buyers: a larger company in the sector, another fund, or a stock market listing. No credible buyer means no deal.
  • Ignoring the debt. More debt raises the return when things go well and can sink the company when they do not.

Practise it

1. A fund invests $50M of equity and wants 3x in five years. It expects $30M of net debt at exit and an exit multiple of 9x. What EBITDA does the company need at exit?

Show the answer

Equity at exit: $50M × 3 = $150M. Enterprise value: $150M + $30M = $180M. EBITDA: $180M ÷ 9 = $20M. A 3x return over five years is about 25% a year, so the next question is whether $20M is realistic from today's starting point.

2. Should a private equity fund buy a chain of 80 gyms?

Show the answer
  • Market: growth, competition between low-cost and premium gyms, member churn across the industry
  • The company: profit per gym, best against worst sites, management, membership trends
  • Value creation: new sites, pricing, cost savings, fixing the weakest gyms
  • Deal and risks: price, debt and return against the target; lease commitments; churn in a downturn

Start with the return: can the fund reach its target at this price under a sensible plan? The trap is describing the market at length and never getting to the return.

Where to practise next

Read the complete guide to private equity cases and what to ask first in a PE case. Then work through a full case: FitHub Gyms (a budget gym chain) or Crescent Dental Labs (can a fund triple its money?).
